title: /respond-html — what a structured artifact looks like
subtitle: A reading-optimized reply that you can react to inline. Try the ✅/💬/❌ buttons on any section, callout, or decision-block. Hit 📋 Copy feedback when done.
bluf: When a chat reply would be a wall of prose with implicit structure (sections, comparisons, decisions), an HTML artifact wins. You scan, react inline on each unit, copy the feedback as markdown, paste it back to chat. This very page is what /respond-html produces for a plan- or proposal-shaped request — and it's the same skeleton you'll see for audits, comparisons, and recommendations.

sections.title: Shape of the artifact
sections.body:
Every response-artifact has the same skeleton: BLUF (bottom-line-up-front) → context → body sections → open questions. The sticky TOC on the left mirrors the H2s; the sticky toolbar on the right shows live reaction counts.

Body sections mix three kinds of reactable units:

  • Sections — each H2 is reactable as a whole.
  • Callouts — boxed inline blocks for decision, tradeoff, risk, recommendation.
  • Decision-blocks — a question with 2–4 mutually exclusive options and a marked recommendation.

Aim for 8–20 reactable units total. Fewer than 8 → the artifact is probably too simple, just reply in chat. More than 20 → reaction-fatigue, split the artifact.

sections.title: Gravity tag picks the aesthetic
sections.body:
Instead of randomly rotating fonts, the skill picks an aesthetic from an 8-row mapping based on the artifact's gravity — how heavy the content is, what kind of decision it carries.

Gravity tagUse whenAesthetic
sternSecurity audit, contract review, money/legalIBM Plex Serif + Sans, oxford blue
decisiveStrategy proposal, roadmap with clear recommendationCrimson Pro + Manrope, jade
balancedComparison, X vs Y tradeoff analysisSource Serif 4 + Geist, deep teal
distinctiveMockup, design proposal, creative briefFraunces + Bricolage Grotesque, deep violet
editorialRoutine plan, project status, recapNewsreader + Hanken Grotesk, vermilion
measuredAudit (non-security), retro, postmortemEB Garamond + Outfit, amber
lightQuick recommendation, single-decision memoLora + Hanken Grotesk, jade
multidimensionalCompound (data + plan, audit + mockup)Spectral + Manrope, deep violet

This page is gravity decisive (a recommendation-shaped intro). Hence Crimson Pro + Manrope + jade. The eyebrow at the top calls it out: Skill intro · /respond-html.

Design call

Two artifacts of the same gravity will look the same. That's intentional — they're the same shape of response. Variation comes from changing the gravity tag to match the actual content, not from randomizing fonts.

sections.title: Callouts and decision-blocks
sections.body:
Four callout types cover most cases:

Tradeoff

Use when you're accepting a cost in exchange for a benefit. "We give up X to get Y." Amber accent.

Risk

Something that could go wrong. "If X, then Y." Red accent.

Recommendation

What should be done. "Do X." Blue accent.

Decision

A choice the reader needs to weigh in on. Neutral accent.

For multi-option choices, use a decision-block — it makes the recommended option visually distinct:

Where should artifacts live on disk?

Project-aware (recommended)

Co-locate with the project being discussed: ~/dev/<project>/.html-answers/<slug>/. Easy to find, naturally scoped, easy to clean up.

One central directory

Everything in ~/dev/html-answers/. Simpler routing, harder to find old artifacts.

Per-session

Date-based directory. Discoverable by time, harder to find by topic.

Rationale: artifacts are usually about a specific project, so co-locating wins on discoverability.

sections.title: Reactions and feedback flow
sections.body:
Every section, callout, and decision-block has a row of buttons auto-injected by the template JS:

  • ✅ — looks good, keep going
  • 💬 — has a comment (a text box appears)
  • ❌ — disagree / wrong / remove

Reactions persist in browser localStorage, so you can react across a session and not lose state on reload. The sticky toolbar shows live counts. When you're done, hit 📋 Copy feedback — it dumps everything as markdown to your clipboard, grouped by section, ready to paste back to chat.

localStorage gotcha

Reactions are keyed by location.pathname. If you validated against http://localhost:8765/ but then open the file via file:///…, the reactions won't carry over — different pathname. The skill's final step always uses open file://<abs-path> for consistency.

sections.title: How this skill chains with others
sections.body:
/respond-html is an orchestrator. For content that fits another skill's wheelhouse, it delegates:

  • Data analysis (JSON / CSV / EDA requests) → /dataviz data mode
  • Process / workflow / architecture diagrams → /dataviz process mode
  • UI component / page mockup → /frontend-design
  • Plan / proposal / audit / comparison → its own response-artifact template (what you're looking at)

After rendering, it always runs /chrome-validate all against the artifact before declaring it ready — catches broken fonts, dead links, layout-integrity bugs, and 0×0 images that screenshots miss.

Tradeoff

Bundled here: /chrome-validate. Not bundled: /dataviz, /frontend-design. If you don't have those installed, /respond-html still works for the four content types its own template handles — the chain just doesn't extend further.

sections.title: Open questions for you
sections.body:
Things worth surfacing for feedback as you try the skill:

  • Aesthetic list size — 8 gravity rows ship. Want to expand (e.g., add "reflective" or "celebratory")?
  • TTL grace — if you wire up the optional cleanup step, 30 days is the default. Should it be longer for long-lived project areas?
  • Generator language — Python locked in for the canonical regeneration script. If you'd prefer Node, the script is small enough to rewrite.
  • Within-gravity variation — currently two decisive plans look identical. Worth adding optional within-row pair swap so consecutive same-gravity artifacts don't feel like a series?

React on this section to flag anything. Defer answers if you'd rather use the skill for a bit first.
